name: Server side tagging
plain: The site sends its analytics to its own server first, which relays it to ad vendors.
meaning: Moves tracking from the browser to the site's cloud container, so blockers cannot see vendor calls and cookies are set by the site's own server. The vendor can still receive IP, user agent, hashed email and click IDs the server chooses to forward.

web.api: Google Tag Manager server container on a first party subdomain; Set-Cookie from server

access.persistence: Server set cookies can last up to 400 days but Safari caps IP mismatched ones at 7 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can send your activity to the site's own server first, then on to ad vendors
limits.user_action: Nothing on your side. It happens as you use a site that routes data through its server
can: Collect your visits on the site's own server
Pass them to ad and analytics vendors
Choose what data each vendor receives, including fewer details
cannot: Be seen or blocked by your browser, since the relay is out of sight
Add details the browser never sent
Work unless the site has set it up
Give vendors your data if the site chooses not to pass it on
limits.reach_label: What the site chooses to pass on

story.what_it_is: A site sends its tracking to its own server first, which passes it on to ad vendors.

marketing.name: Server side tagging
marketing.pitch: Google pitches it as moving tags to a server container for faster pages, more control and better data.

story.for_you: You never see it. Instead of loading many vendor scripts, the page sends one stream to the site's own server. Blockers cannot see vendor calls, and cookies are set by the site's own server.
story.for_makers: Pages load faster and the company controls what each vendor gets. It also gets around blockers and short cookie limits. The server can still forward IP, hashed email and click IDs.

use_cases.example: A shop sends all events to its own server, then to Google Analytics and Meta, so pages load faster.
An advertiser sets a first party cookie from its own server, so it lasts longer than a script cookie.
A game store sends purchase events through its server to ad networks, with no vendor script on the page.
A publisher removes dozens of ad scripts from the page and sends data from its server.
A company hashes email on its server and drops IP before sharing, to cut what vendors see.
A retailer adds server events to fill gaps when shoppers use blockers.

risks: Cannot be blocked in your browser
Company decides what each vendor sees

technical_bounds: Server must forward data on its own authority
Safari caps cookies from servers on different IP ranges
Browser mitigations like Safari 27 IP blocking do not see server to server calls

abuse: Evading blockers, covert hashed email forwarding

history.change: Google Tag Manager server side tagging announced
